body_markdown:
It’s the spookiest week of the year, and Rolls-Royce has timed it to perfection to remind us that the Silver Ghost made its first appearance 120 years ago.


To be pedantic, the 40/50 H.P., which would become known as “the best car in the world,” didn’t actually make its debut until November 15, 1906 at the 5th International Motor Exhibition held at London’s Olympia.


Two examples of the new 7.0-liter, six-cylinder motored car were revealed on the Rolls-Royce stand, alongside the earlier four-cylinder 20 H.P. and the six-cylinder 30 H.P. The side-valve engine was designed to be exceptionally smooth-running, with a seven-bearing crankshaft and full-pressure lubrication. It even boasted twin spark plugs for each cylinder.


The show cars weren’t quite finished, however, so His Majesty’s Motoring Press would have to wait until 1907 to drive the car. It was then that *The Autocar* magazine gave it that famous world-beating review. *Country Life* called it, “The quintessence of all that a car ought to be”.


Rolls-Royce


Claude Johnson, Rolls-Royce’s Commercial Managing Director, had developed a habit of naming each individual car the company produced. For chassis number 60551, which was finished in silver paintwork with silver-plated fittings, he came up with the moniker “Silver Ghost.” Soon after, other owners adopted this name for their own[40/50 H.P. models](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/rolls-royce-phantom-celebrates-centenary/) .


Johnson, known to all as CJ, also knew that success in competition would be key to sales, so the Silver Ghost was entered into[trialing competitions](https://www.hagerty.com/media/magazine-features/hagerty-magazine/englands-vintage-sports-car-club-mud-warriors/) such as the Scottish Reliability Trial, the London-Edinburgh Run, the Austrian Alpine Trial, and even the Spanish Grand Prix. Securing victory in these endurance events cemented Rolls-Royce’s reputation for reliability. Further proof, if it was needed, came when the car was driven from London to Glasgow 27 times—a distance of 15,000 miles.


Before long, the Silver Ghost would become *the* car of the rich and famous. Playboy pilot and yachtsman Tommy Sopwith owned one, as did Baron Alfred de Rothschild, Lord Pirrie, chairman of shipbuilders Harland & Wolff, and Sir Winston Churchill. Across the pond, Howard Hughes added a Silver Ghost to his collection; in Australia opera singer Dame Nellie Melba had one, and in India the government ordered no less than eight landaulette-bodied cars in time for a tour by King George VI and Queen Mary.


The Silver Ghost endured until 1926, by which time almost 8000 examples had been built; it’s estimated that around 1500 cars are still going strong. As recently as 2013, 47 Silver Ghosts retraced the route of the 1913 Alpine Trial, while in 2021 chassis number 1701 recreated its London-Edinburgh run, locked into top gear just as it did more than a century earlier.


“The Silver Ghost occupies a special place in Rolls-Royce history,” says Andrew Ball, Head of Corporate Relations and Heritage at Rolls-Royce. “Its engineering achievements established a reputation for refinement, reliability and excellence that was extraordinary even by today’s standards. Equally remarkable was the response it inspired among those who experienced it, and the expectations it created of Rolls-Royce itself. One hundred and twenty years later, those expectations continue to define the standards to which the marque holds itself.”
